sections.html:
A Lyon County city, Fernley belongs to the Reno-Tahoe-Sparks metropolitan area and stands where Interstate 80, US Alternate 50 and US Alternate 95 come together. As of July 1, 2025, an estimated 26,214 people live here. Elevation is about 4,636 feet, and the city covers 128.39 square miles, of which 121.65 is land.

It began in 1904 as an agricultural and ranching community and incorporated on July 1, 2001. Buyers may compare a house here with others around Reno. Fernley has its own flood history, though, and that is the topic to be ready for.

On January 5, 2008, the north embankment of the Truckee Canal failed inside Fernley after a winter storm. The Truckee-Carson Irrigation District reports that approximately 590 homes flooded. About 3,500 people were evacuated, and 3 to 6 feet of water filled houses. A dam safety review found that water ran through the breach for up to 9 hours and reached depths up to 8 feet in places.

Repairs were made in February 2008 and the canal reopened in March 2008. The canal serves approximately 3,000 water right holders, including landowners, farmers and the City of Fernley. Since the breach its flows have been held under water-level limits, and the later lining project allows flows above 500 cubic feet per second.

The irrigation district's Public Safety Project included 3.56 miles of full-prism lining and replacement of the Fernley Check Structure, among other work. A record of decision came in December 2020, construction started in November 2022, and the district declared the project substantially complete in July 2024.

It can. Expect a buyer or a lender to ask if your parcel lies in a flood zone or ever had water damage. Nevada's disclosure form requires a seller to state known conditions that materially affect the property, which means a house that took on water in 2008 gets described plainly, repairs and claims included.

Ask the City of Fernley or your insurance agent about the flood zone status of your parcel. A standard homeowner's policy excludes flood damage. If you are not sure what yours says, read it before you list.

  • Collect repair records and permits from any post-flood work.
  • Ask your insurer what your policy covers.
  • Tell buyers what you know. Nevada law allows treble damages when a known defect goes undisclosed.

sections.h2: Wear and tear a buyer will notice
sections.html:
Fernley has a cold desert climate with about 5 inches of rain a year, cold winters with some snow and hot, very dry summers. Sun and dry air wear down roofing, fences and paint, while winter cold can strain pipes and heating equipment.

Inspection reports will flag those items for a buyer with a loan, who may ask for repairs. Someone paying cash can accept the house as is. Many owners in the area also commute toward Reno, Sparks or the industrial park, so mention how long your address takes to reach the interstate.

Under NRS 113.130, a Fernley seller fills out Nevada's Seller's Real Property Disclosure Form. Transfer tax comes to $1.95 per $500 of value, the state base. Washoe, Churchill and Clark counties alone carry extras, and Lyon County is not one of them. Ask the title company to confirm the total.

A declaration of value travels with the deed to the county recorder. Since NRS 375 permits charging either party, settle the payer in the contract.

sections.h2: How Lyon County bills property tax
sections.html:
Fernley parcels follow the Nevada schedule, billed by Lyon County. Payment dates: third Monday of August, then first Mondays of October, January and March. NRS 361.483 starts the late penalty at 4 percent and permits installments only where a parcel's tax tops $100.

A single-family primary residence can claim the partial abatement in NRS 361.4723, holding yearly growth near 3 percent. A house rented to others does not qualify. If you are selling a former rental, expect the next bill to look different from the last one.

Ahead of closing, check with the Lyon County offices on each installment for your parcel. What is open gets paid from your proceeds by the title company, which also divides the current installment between buyer and seller.

You can clear an unpaid balance through the sale itself. Phone the Lyon County offices, learn which installments are open and request the amount in writing. Your proceeds cover it at closing, so no cash is needed beforehand. Penalties keep adding up until the balance is paid, which is one more reason a quicker closing can help.

Inherited houses add a wrinkle. Heirs often discover that an installment or two went unpaid while the estate was being settled. Sort that out before the contract is signed, and tell the title company so nothing surprises anyone at the table.

Few steps are involved. A buyer tours the house and offers. Title work verifies ownership and liens. After you sign the contract and disclosure, closing happens at a title or escrow office, and the deed plus its declaration of value are sent to the county recorder.

Houses with flood history deserve one extra conversation up front. If the buyer hears about the 2008 water damage, the repairs and any insurance claim from you, the file is clean from the start. Repair records and permits make that talk easy, and a house with no paperwork can still sell, as long as you describe what you know.

Tenants, probate and unpermitted work can slow any sale, so mention them at the first call. A cash buyer can often work around them, but only if the facts are known early.

Because a cash buyer takes out no mortgage, nothing waits for an appraisal or underwriting. Your duties stay the same: finish the disclosure, deliver clear title and settle any loan or lien at closing, with the deed filed afterward.

Cash Home Buyers reviews the house as it stands, promises no price in advance and charges you nothing if you decline. Sellers of homes with flood history, deferred repairs, inherited status or tenants often prefer this route to a repair list and a listing period.

  • Look for repair records, permits and insurance claim papers dating from the flood years.
  • Have the deed and newest tax bill ready.
  • Note every known defect for the disclosure.

faqs.a: A levee on the north side of the Truckee Canal breached on January 5, 2008 after a winter storm. The irrigation district says approximately 590 homes were flooded.
Yes. Emergency repairs were made in 2008, and the irrigation district's Public Safety Project, including 3.56 miles of full-prism lining, was declared substantially complete in July 2024.

faqs.q: What transfer tax do Fernley sellers pay?
faqs.a: The state base rate of $1.95 per $500 of value applies, since Lyon County has no add-on. Confirm the amount with your title company.

faqs.q: What are the Lyon County installment dates?
faqs.a: The third Monday of August, then the first Mondays of October, January and March. Installments are available when taxes exceed $100.

faqs.q: Do I have to disclose the 2008 flood when I sell a Fernley house?
faqs.a: If your house took on water, yes, describe it, along with repairs and any claims. Nevada law allows treble damages when a known defect goes undisclosed.
